cards.front: Define a rational number. What are the conditions?
cards.back: A rational number is any number that can be written as p/q where: (1) p and q are both integers, and (2) q ≠ 0 (denominator is never zero). Examples: 3/7, −4/5, 0/1 (= 0), 6/1 (= 6), −3/−7 (= 3/7). All fractions, all integers, and all negative fractions are rational numbers.
cards.memory_hook: RATIONAL = RATIO of integers. p/q is a RATIO of two integers. Remember: q can NEVER be 0 — dividing by zero is the one rule you can NEVER break in maths!

cards.front: Is every integer a rational number? Give an example.
cards.back: Yes — every integer n is a rational number because it can be written as n/1. Examples: 5 = 5/1, −8 = −8/1, 0 = 0/1. So the set of rational numbers includes all integers, all positive fractions, and all negative fractions. Rational numbers are an extension of the number system beyond just integers.
cards.memory_hook: INTEGER → RATIONAL is easy: just put /1 under it! 7 → 7/1. −3 → −3/1. 0 → 0/1. Every integer is a rational number in disguise — wearing a '/1' costume!

cards.front: What is the standard form of a rational number? What are its two conditions?
cards.back: A rational number p/q is in standard form when: (1) The denominator q is positive (q > 0). (2) The HCF of |p| (absolute value of numerator) and q = 1 — meaning numerator and denominator share no common factor other than 1. To reduce to standard form: step 1 — make denominator positive; step 2 — divide both by HCF. Example: −8/12 → HCF(8,12)=4 → −2/3 (standard form).
cards.memory_hook: Standard Form = POSITIVE denominator + FULLY REDUCED. Think of it as tidying up: the denominator must be 'upright' (positive) and the fraction must be 'trimmed' (no common factors). A neat, tidy rational number!

cards.front: Where do positive and negative rational numbers lie on the number line?
cards.back: On the number line: positive rational numbers lie to the RIGHT of zero; negative rational numbers lie to the LEFT of zero. Zero (0) is neither positive nor negative — it sits at the centre. The further right, the greater the value. The further left, the smaller (more negative) the value. All positive rationals > 0 > all negative rationals.
cards.memory_hook: NUMBER LINE: RIGHT = POSITIVE (richer!), LEFT = NEGATIVE (poorer!). Think of it as a financial scale — positive money is to the right, debt is to the left, and 0 is breaking even!

cards.front: How many rational numbers exist between any two rational numbers?
cards.back: Infinitely many rational numbers exist between any two distinct rational numbers. For example, between 1/3 and 1/2, there are infinitely many rational numbers including 5/12, 7/18, 2/5, etc. This property — that rational numbers are 'dense' (infinitely many between any two) — distinguishes them from integers, where there may be no integer between two consecutive integers.
cards.memory_hook: INFINITE rationals between any two = the number line is INFINITELY CROWDED between any two points. It's like zooming into a Google Map — no matter how close two points seem, you can always zoom in more and find more points between them!

cards.front: What is the additive inverse of a rational number? Give an example.
cards.back: The additive inverse of a rational number p/q is −p/q. When you add a number to its additive inverse, the result is 0. Example: additive inverse of 3/7 is −3/7, because 3/7 + (−3/7) = 0. Additive inverse of −5/8 is 5/8. The additive inverse is also called the 'opposite' of the number. Every rational number has exactly one additive inverse.
cards.memory_hook: ADDITIVE INVERSE = the opposite that cancels you out to ZERO. It's your maths 'nemesis' — you two together equal nothing! 3/7 + its nemesis (−3/7) = 0. Perfect cancellation!

cards.front: What is the reciprocal (multiplicative inverse) of a rational number? Give an example.
cards.back: The reciprocal of p/q is q/p — flip the numerator and denominator. When a number is multiplied by its reciprocal, the result is 1. Example: reciprocal of 3/7 is 7/3, because (3/7) × (7/3) = 21/21 = 1. Reciprocal of −2/5 is −5/2. Reciprocal of 4 (=4/1) is 1/4. Zero (0/1) has NO reciprocal because 1/0 is undefined.
cards.memory_hook: RECIPROCAL = FLIP IT! p/q → q/p. Think of flipping a pancake — what was on top goes to bottom and vice versa. And multiplied together they give 1 — a perfect pair!

cards.front: What is the rule for adding/subtracting rational numbers with different denominators?
cards.back: To add or subtract rational numbers with different denominators: Step 1 — Find the LCM of the denominators. Step 2 — Convert each fraction to an equivalent fraction with the LCM as denominator. Step 3 — Add or subtract the numerators (keep denominator as LCM). Step 4 — Reduce to standard form. Example: 1/4 + 1/6: LCM=12 → 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12.
cards.memory_hook: ADD/SUB rational numbers: LCM → Convert → Operate → Reduce. Remember: LCOR! You cannot add fractions with different denominators any more than you can add apples and oranges — you need a COMMON unit (denominator) first!

cards.front: State the sign rule for multiplication of rational numbers.
cards.back: Sign rules for multiplication: (positive) × (positive) = positive. (negative) × (negative) = positive. (positive) × (negative) = negative. (negative) × (positive) = negative. Summary: SAME signs → POSITIVE result. DIFFERENT signs → NEGATIVE result. Example: (−3/4) × (−2/5) = +6/20 = 3/10 (both negative → positive). (3/4) × (−2/5) = −6/20 = −3/10 (different signs → negative).
cards.memory_hook: SIGNS: Same → Smile (positive +). Different → Disagree (negative −). Two negatives = two people disagreeing with each other's disagreement = they AGREE = positive! Mathematical peacemaking!

cards.front: How do you divide one rational number by another?
cards.back: To divide p/q by r/s: multiply p/q by the RECIPROCAL of r/s. Formula: (p/q) ÷ (r/s) = (p/q) × (s/r) = ps/qr. Remember the KCF rule: KEEP the first fraction, CHANGE ÷ to ×, FLIP the second fraction. Example: (3/5) ÷ (2/7) = (3/5) × (7/2) = 21/10. Apply sign rules for the final answer.
cards.memory_hook: KCF = Keep, Change, Flip. (3/5) ÷ (2/7): KEEP 3/5, CHANGE ÷ to ×, FLIP 2/7 to 7/2 → (3/5) × (7/2) = 21/10. KCF is your division superpower — never forget it!

cards.front: How do you compare two rational numbers with different denominators?
cards.back: To compare rational numbers p/q and r/s: Step 1 — Find LCM of q and s. Step 2 — Convert both to equivalent fractions with LCM denominator: p/q = (p × LCM/q) / LCM and r/s = (r × LCM/s) / LCM. Step 3 — Compare the new numerators — larger numerator = larger rational number. Example: Compare −3/4 and −5/6. LCM=12. −3/4 = −9/12, −5/6 = −10/12. Since −9 > −10, we have −3/4 > −5/6.
cards.memory_hook: Compare rationals: LCM → Same denominator → Compare numerators. Think of making all fractions 'speak the same language' (same denominator) before comparing. You can't compare apples and oranges — convert to grams first!

cards.front: How do you find rational numbers between two given rational numbers?
cards.back: Method: Step 1 — Find LCM of denominators and convert. If not enough numbers between numerators, multiply both fractions by a suitable number. Step 2 — List fractions with numerators between the two converted numerators. Example: Between 1/3 and 1/2. LCM=6: 2/6 and 3/6. Only one integer between 2 and 3. Multiply both by 5: 10/30 and 15/30. Rational numbers: 11/30, 12/30 (=2/5), 13/30, 14/30 (=7/15).
cards.memory_hook: Finding rationals between two: ZOOM IN by multiplying both by a bigger number. Like zooming into a map — suddenly many more locations appear between two points that seemed close!

cards.front: Why is 0 a special rational number? How does it behave in operations?
cards.back: 0 is special because: (1) 0 is a rational number (0 = 0/1). (2) 0 is neither positive nor negative. (3) 0 is the ADDITIVE IDENTITY: any rational number + 0 = that number. (4) 0 × (any rational) = 0. (5) 0 ÷ (any non-zero rational) = 0. (6) You CANNOT divide by 0 — it is undefined. (7) 0 has no multiplicative inverse (reciprocal) because 1/0 is undefined.
cards.memory_hook: ZERO: Identity for addition (adds nothing), Destroyer for multiplication (everything becomes 0), FORBIDDEN as a denominator or divisor. Zero is the wildcard of rational numbers — powerful in some ways, impossible in others!

cards.front: Reduce −15/35 to standard form. Show all steps.
cards.back: Step 1: Check the denominator — 35 is positive ✓. Step 2: Find HCF(15, 35). Factors of 15: 1,3,5,15. Factors of 35: 1,5,7,35. HCF = 5. Step 3: Divide both by 5: −15÷5 / 35÷5 = −3/7. Step 4: Check — denominator 7 is positive ✓; HCF(3,7) = 1 ✓. Answer: Standard form of −15/35 = −3/7.
cards.memory_hook: −15/35 → HCF is 5 → divide both → −3/7. Steps: positive denominator? ✓ → find HCF → divide both → done. Two-step tidy-up for every standard form problem!

cards.front: Calculate: (−2/3) + (4/5). Show steps.
cards.back: Step 1: Different denominators → find LCM(3,5) = 15. Step 2: Convert −2/3: multiply by 5/5 → −10/15. Step 3: Convert 4/5: multiply by 3/3 → 12/15. Step 4: Add: (−10 + 12)/15 = 2/15. Step 5: Check standard form: denominator 15 > 0 ✓; HCF(2,15) = 1 ✓. Answer: (−2/3) + (4/5) = 2/15.
cards.memory_hook: LCM of 3 and 5 = 15. −2/3 = −10/15, 4/5 = 12/15. −10 + 12 = 2. Answer: 2/15. LCOR in action: LCM(15) → Convert → Operate(−10+12=2) → Result(2/15)!

cards.front: Calculate: (−3/7) × (14/9). Show steps.
cards.back: Step 1: Multiply numerators: (−3) × 14 = −42. Step 2: Multiply denominators: 7 × 9 = 63. Step 3: Result: −42/63. Step 4: Reduce — HCF(42,63) = 21. Divide both by 21: −2/3. Step 5: Signs — one negative, one positive → negative ✓. Answer: (−3/7) × (14/9) = −2/3.
cards.memory_hook: PRO TIP: Cancel BEFORE multiplying to save work! −3/7 × 14/9: 3 and 9 share factor 3 (→ 1 and 3); 14 and 7 share factor 7 (→ 2 and 1). So: (−1/1) × (2/3) = −2/3. Cross-cancellation = maths efficiency!

cards.front: Calculate: (−4/5) ÷ (8/15). Show full steps.
cards.back: Step 1: Apply KCF — Keep (−4/5), Change (÷ to ×), Flip (8/15 to 15/8). → (−4/5) × (15/8). Step 2: Multiply numerators: (−4) × 15 = −60. Step 3: Multiply denominators: 5 × 8 = 40. Step 4: Result: −60/40. Step 5: HCF(60,40) = 20. Divide both: −3/2. Answer: (−4/5) ÷ (8/15) = −3/2.
cards.memory_hook: KCF: Keep −4/5, Change ÷ to ×, Flip 8/15 to 15/8. Then: −4×15 = −60, 5×8 = 40, −60/40 = −3/2. Or cancel first: 4 and 8 → 1 and 2; 15 and 5 → 3 and 1. Answer: −3/2. Same result, less work!

cards.front: Compare −5/6 and −7/9. Which is greater?
cards.back: Step 1: Find LCM(6,9) = 18. Step 2: Convert −5/6: multiply by 3/3 → −15/18. Step 3: Convert −7/9: multiply by 2/2 → −14/18. Step 4: Compare numerators: −15 vs −14. Since −14 > −15 (less negative), we have −14/18 > −15/18. Step 5: Therefore −7/9 > −5/6. Answer: −7/9 is greater than −5/6.
cards.memory_hook: Comparing negatives TRIPS students! −14 > −15 even though 14 < 15. On the number line: −14/18 is closer to 0 than −15/18, so it is GREATER. With negatives: LESS negative = GREATER value. Think of debt: owing ₹14 is better than owing ₹15!

cards.front: Find two rational numbers between −1/2 and 0.
cards.back: Step 1: Convert to same denominator. −1/2 = −1/2 and 0 = 0/2. We need numbers between −1/2 and 0/2, but −1 to 0 has nothing in between as integers. Step 2: Multiply both by 4: −1/2 = −4/8 and 0 = 0/8. Step 3: Numbers between −4/8 and 0/8: −3/8, −2/8 (= −1/4), −1/8. Step 4: Two rational numbers between −1/2 and 0 are −3/8 and −1/4.
cards.memory_hook: Between −1/2 and 0? ZOOM IN by multiplying by 4 → −4/8 to 0/8 → pick −3/8 and −2/8. Zooming into the number line between negatives works just like between positives!

cards.front: Why does the definition of rational numbers require q ≠ 0? What goes wrong if q = 0?
cards.back: If q = 0, then p/q means p ÷ 0 — dividing by zero. Division is defined as finding how many times the divisor fits into the dividend. No number (or infinite numbers) can be multiplied by 0 to give p (if p ≠ 0), so p/0 has no defined value. If p = 0, then 0/0 is indeterminate (any number × 0 = 0, so no unique answer). Division by zero creates logical contradictions in mathematics. Therefore q = 0 is strictly forbidden.
cards.memory_hook: q ≠ 0 = the GOLDEN RULE of rational numbers. Breaking it = mathematical chaos. It's like dividing a pizza among 0 people — how much does each person get? The question makes no sense! Zero denominator = mathematical nonsense.
